title: One small mercy
hook: on a bad day, look for one small mercy

segments.voice: Yesterday, a dish on the doorstep. Your line was someone else's hands. Did you say yes to one offer of help, even a small one? Day seven hundred forty-four.

The alarm didn't go off. The train sat in a tunnel, going nowhere. There was a hard email before lunch, and a call from the clinic that ended with, we'll need to run more tests. Then, on the walk home, a stranger held the door at the corner shop, and there was one of the good rolls left, still warm. Small. Nearly nothing. It didn't fix the day. But it was there. An old book of grief has a line about exactly that kind of thing, set right in the middle of its sorrow.
screen: `A DAY GOING WRONG.` → `ONE WARM ROLL.` → `A LINE IN A BOOK OF GRIEF.`

segments.voice: First, where the line lives. Lamentations is a book of poems over a ruined city. It is full of anguish. In the third chapter the poet says, "thou hast removed my soul far off from peace: I forgat prosperity." He has forgotten what good even feels like. Second, the turn. A few verses later, nothing outside has changed. The city is still in ruins. But he writes, "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope." And then: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning." Notice the verb. He recalls. He doesn't deny the ruins; he turns his attention, on purpose, to something else that is also true. Third, the word. The Hebrew behind mercies is hesed. English Bibles translate it in different ways: mercy, kindness, lovingkindness. Jews and Christians read these lines as being about God's faithfulness. Someone with no faith in God can still borrow the move underneath: recall one thing that was kind today. Fourth, why small. This is not a silver lining. Last week, the line was growth isn't required, and that still stands. A small mercy doesn't explain the bad day or make it worth it. It doesn't cancel the test results. It just sits next to them: a warm roll, a held door, a text from a friend. The poet in Lamentations doesn't stop lamenting after this verse. The book goes on grieving. He has simply found one thing to hold while it does.
screen: `A BOOK OF POEMS OVER RUINS.` · `THIS I RECALL TO MY MIND.` · `HESED: MERCY, KINDNESS.` · `NOT A SILVER LINING.` · then, large: `ONE SMALL MERCY.`

segments.voice: Settle. Let today, or yesterday if today has barely started, play back for a moment, hard parts included. Don't argue with them. Then look for one small mercy in it. Small enough to miss: a kind word, hot water, a song in a shop, a minute when nothing hurt. When you find it, stay with it. Name it once, quietly. If you pray, you can give thanks for it in your own words, or with the line from Lamentations: they are new every morning. Then breathe beside it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Hesed, the Hebrew word behind mercies in Lamentations: God's mercies, new every morning, recalled on purpose inside the ruin. Today's word.
Your line: they are new every morning. Tonight, before sleep, find one from today, however tiny, and name it. Day seven hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Jewish and Christian readers return to Lamentations 3:22–23, 'they are new every morning', on hard days, and some people keep a nightly habit of naming one good thing from the day.

original.note: Hebrew, from Lamentations 3:22, where the King James 'mercies' translates this word in the plural.

trapdoor: what you thought: a small mercy is a silver lining that makes the bad day worth it.
what it means: one kind thing noticed beside the hard things, without explaining them away.
what a scholar hears: Lamentations 3:21–23, the turn in the middle of the book, where 'mercies' renders hesed, a word English Bibles also give as kindness and lovingkindness.
